sandhi.note: a + a → ā. The m of अमर्षम् simply joins the following vowel.
Final t, voiced to d, becomes the nasal n before the nasal n of निशुम्भः (an optional rule, taken here).
-aḥ before a: the s (as रु) becomes u, a + u → o, and the following a is absorbed (avagraha).

samasa.sense: the main asura host now being cut down
samasa.alt: महत् becomes महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya.

samasa.literal: with the army of the asuras

morph.note: Passive present stem हन्य- (√हन् + yak) with the participle suffix -मान: ‘being slain’, an action still going on.
Present participle उद्वहत्, nom. sg. m. उद्वहन्: ‘bearing up’ indignation, i.e. swelling with it.
Imperfect with the augment अ placed after the prefix: अभि + अ-धावत् → अभ्यधावत् (i before a becomes y).

mantras.anvaya: अथ हन्यमानं महासैन्यं विलोक्य अमर्षम् उद्वहन् निशुम्भः मुख्यया असुरसेनया (सह) अभ्यधावत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The absolutive विलोक्य and the participle उद्वहन् lead up to the main verb अभ्यधावत्; मुख्यया असुरसेनया is an instrumental of accompaniment (सह understood).
mantras.lit: Seeing the great army being slain, bearing indignation, Niśumbha then rushed forward with the chief asura army.
mantras.tr: Seeing his great army being cut down, Niśumbha, seething with fury, charged forward with the pick of the asura host.

comm.t: Niśumbha, the younger brother, takes the field first, with the best of the remaining troops. अमर्ष is the anger of one who cannot bear an affront or a defeat.
Chapter 9 is named for him (निशुम्भवधः): his charge here opens the battle that ends with his death (9.34–36).

sandhi.note: a + a → ā; visarga before t becomes s.
-āḥ before a voiced sound: the s (as रु) becomes y, and that y is then dropped before a consonant, leaving क्रुद्धा.
a + o → au. A vārttika also allows o here before ओष्ठ in a compound (संदष्टोष्ठ); the Gita Press has the regular au.

samasa.literal: by whom the folds of the lips are bitten
samasa.sense: grinding their lips in fury — a stock gesture of rage

morph.note: Perfect of √या (ययुः, 3rd plural) with the prefixes उप + आ: ‘came up to, approached’.
संदष्ट is the past participle of सम् + √दंश् ‘to bite’, with the nasal of the root lost before -ta.
Infinitive of purpose after a verb of motion: ‘came … to kill’.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य अग्रतः तथा पृष्ठे पार्श्वयोः च संदष्टौष्ठपुटाः क्रुद्धाः महासुराः देवीं हन्तुम् उपाययुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Place adverbials (अग्रतः, पृष्ठे, पार्श्वयोः, all governed by तस्य) frame the subject महासुराः with its two qualifiers; हन्तुम् gives the purpose of उपाययुः.
mantras.lit: In front of him, and likewise behind, and on both sides, great asuras, biting their lips, enraged, came up to kill the Devī.
mantras.tr: Before him, behind him and on either flank the great asuras advanced, biting their lips in rage, bent on killing the Goddess.

comm.t: Niśumbha’s champions form a guard on every side of him as they close on the Devī. Biting the lips is the epic sign of fury.

sandhi.note: Before the sibilant ś the visarga stands (the change to ś is optional and not made here). शुम्भः + अपि → शुम्भोऽपि, with avagraha for the elided a.
After ai (not a/ā) the final s (as रु) appears as r before a voiced sound.
Final m before k is written as anusvāra; the t of कोपात् stays unvoiced before k and is only written together with कृत्वा.

morph.note: Perfect of आ + √गम्: reduplicated ज-गाम (the guttural g of the root becomes j in the reduplication), with vṛddhi in the 3rd singular.
Absolutive: an action finished before the main verb. Śumbha came after doing battle with the Mothers.
Past participle of √वृ ‘to cover’: ‘covered, surrounded’, with its agent स्वबलैः in the instrumental.

mantras.anvaya: महावीर्यः शुम्भः अपि मातृभिः तु युद्धं कृत्वा स्वबलैः वृतः कोपात् चण्डिकां निहन्तुम् आजगाम।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause शुम्भः अपि … आजगाम; the absolutive phrase मातृभिः युद्धं कृत्वा precedes it in time, and निहन्तुम् gives the purpose.
mantras.lit: Śumbha too, of great valour, surrounded by his own forces, came to slay Caṇḍikā out of anger, having done battle with the Mothers.
mantras.tr: Mighty Śumbha too came on, ringed by his own troops, to slay Caṇḍikā in his wrath, after doing battle with the Mothers.

comm.t: The elder brother joins the attack. The Mothers (मातृ) are the śaktis of the gods who joined the Devī in chapter 8 (Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī); Śumbha has been fighting them, and now turns on Caṇḍikā herself.
The Mothers remain on the field through this chapter; at its end (9.38–40) they are named again as they destroy the remaining asuras.

After o the final s (as रु) appears as r before a vowel.

samasa.sense: of the two brothers together (hence the dual)

morph.note: Imperfect of √अस्, with the inserted ī of the root class (आस्-ई-त्): ‘was’.
Present participle वर्षत्, genitive dual. It agrees with the two brothers (शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः) and, through इव, with the two clouds: the brothers rain arrows as two clouds rain water.
Instrumental of association: युद्धं देव्या ‘battle with the Devī’, without सह.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देव्या शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः (च) अतीव युद्धम् आसीत्, (तयोः) मेघयोः इव अतीव उग्रं शरवर्षं वर्षतोः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause is युद्धम् आसीत्; the participle वर्षतोः, agreeing with शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, takes शरवर्षम् as its object, and मेघयोः इव is the simile. Alternatively शरवर्षम् is nominative in apposition to युद्धम् (‘a most fierce rain of arrows, as of two clouds raining’); the sense is the same.
mantras.lit: Then there was an exceedingly (fierce) battle of the Devī with Śumbha and Niśumbha, (the two) raining an exceedingly fierce shower of arrows, like two clouds raining.
mantras.tr: Then a furious battle broke out between the Goddess and Śumbha and Niśumbha, who poured on her a terrible shower of arrows, like two storm-clouds pouring rain.
mantras.tr_note: ‘On her’ and ‘storm-’ make the simile explicit in English; the Sanskrit has only ‘like two clouds raining’.

comm.t: Both brothers now fight the Devī together. The simile of the two rain-clouds pictures the volleys of arrows falling as thick as monsoon rain.

flags.uncertain: Construction of शरवर्षम्: object of वर्षतोः (taken here) or nominative in apposition to युद्धम्. Both are grammatical and give the same picture.

sandhi.note: a + a → ā. Final n before ś becomes the palatal ñ, and the ś after it becomes ch (an optional change, taken here): अस्ताञ्छरान्.
Final n before t becomes ṃs (anusvāra + s). (The word appears as छरां- because its ś has already become ch after अस्ताञ्.)

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi; vowel sandhi inside compounds
sandhi.note: After ai the visarga appears as r before a vowel. Inside the compounds: शस्त्र + ओघ → शस्त्रौघ (a + o → au); असुर + ईश्वर → असुरेश्वर (a + ī → e); likewise स्वशर + उत्कर → स्वशरोत्कर (a + u → o).

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (its first member स्वशर is a karmadhāraya: स्वे शराः)
samasa.literal: with heaps of her own arrows
samasa.sense: with volleys of her own arrows

samasa.literal: the two lords of the asuras

morph.note: Perfect of √छिद्: reduplicated चि-च्छेद, with guṇa (i → e) in the 3rd singular.
Past participle of √अस् ‘to throw’ (not √अस् ‘to be’): अस्त ‘thrown, shot’, with its agent ताभ्याम् in the instrumental.
Periphrastic perfect, used for curādi and causative stems: ताडय- + आम् + आस (perfect of √अस्).

mantras.anvaya: चण्डिका ताभ्याम् अस्तान् शरान् स्वशरोत्करैः चिच्छेद, असुरेश्वरौ च शस्त्रौघैः अङ्गेषु ताडयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two main verbs joined by च: चिच्छेद (object शरान्, qualified by the participle phrase ताभ्याम् अस्तान्) and ताडयामास (object असुरेश्वरौ).
mantras.lit: Caṇḍikā cut the arrows shot by those two with masses of her own arrows, and struck the two lords of the asuras on their limbs with floods of weapons.
mantras.tr: Caṇḍikā cut down the arrows the two of them shot with volleys of her own, and struck the two asura lords all over their bodies with a torrent of weapons.

comm.t: The Devī answers both brothers at once: she destroys their arrows in flight and then wounds them both. The duals (ताभ्याम्, असुरेश्वरौ) keep the two brothers fighting side by side.
Caṇḍikā, ‘the fierce one’, is the name the Devī Māhātmya uses most for her in battle. Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name (755, चण्डिका); the two works remain distinct.
